parts.problem_md:
Mr Shapesphere, a history teacher, records the time, to the nearest minute, that it takes him to mark each of his students' essays. The table shows some of the results.

| Time (minutes) | 0 – 10 | 11 – 30 | 31 – 35 | 36 – 50 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 7 | 16 | 4 |   |

The histogram represents all of the times. No scale is shown on the frequency density axis.

![Histogram with time in minutes from 0 to 55 on the horizontal axis and frequency density on the vertical axis, with tick marks but no numbers. Bars from 0 to 10.5, 10.5 to 30.5, 30.5 to 35.5 and 35.5 to 50.5. The bars from 10.5 to 30.5 and 30.5 to 35.5 are the same height; the bar from 35.5 to 50.5 is three quarters of that height](assets/001-histogram-with-time-in-minutes-from-0-to-55-on-t.png)

Find the number of essays that took him from 36 to 50 minutes to mark.
parts.solution_md:
The times are recorded to the nearest minute, so the class 11 – 30 has boundaries 10.5 and 30.5, and a width of 20. Find its frequency density

$\text{Frequency density} = \frac{16}{20} = 0 . 8$

**[M1]**

This fixes the scale: the bar for 11 – 30 is at 0.8

![Histogram with time from 0 to 55 minutes and frequency density from 0 to 1. Bars: 0 to 10.5 height 0.667, 10.5 to 30.5 height 0.8, 30.5 to 35.5 height 0.8, 35.5 to 50.5 height 0.6](assets/002-histogram-with-time-from-0-to-55-minutes-and-fre.png)

The bar for 36 – 50 is three quarters of the height of the 11 – 30 bar

$\text{Frequency density for 36 – 50} = 0 . 6$

The class 36 – 50 has boundaries 35.5 and 50.5, so its width is 15

$\text{Frequency} = 0 . 6 \times 15$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **9 essays**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Frequency density of a known class found using class boundaries, e.g. $\frac{16}{20}$ or $\frac{4}{5}$.
> 
> **M1**: Frequency density of the 36 – 50 bar (0.6) multiplied by its class width.
> 
> **A1**: 9.

parts.problem_md: Estimate the number of essays that took him between 20 and 40 minutes to mark.
parts.solution_md:
![Histogram with time from 0 to 55 minutes and frequency density from 0 to 1. Bars: 0 to 10.5 height 0.667, 10.5 to 30.5 height 0.8, 30.5 to 35.5 height 0.8, 35.5 to 50.5 height 0.6. The region from 20 to 40 is shaded](assets/003-histogram-with-time-from-0-to-55-minutes-and-fre.png)

Assuming the times are spread evenly within each class, take the part of each class that lies between 20 and 40

$11 -- 30 \text{:} \frac{30.5-20}{20} \times 16 = 8 . 4$

$31 -- 35 \text{:} 4$

$36 -- 50 \text{:} \frac{40-35.5}{15} \times 9 = 2 . 7$

**[M1]**

Add the three parts

$8 . 4 + 4 + 2 . 7 = 15 . 1$

**[M1]**

A number of essays is a whole number

**Final answer:** **15 essays**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct proportion of at least one partial class, e.g. $\frac{10.5}{20} \times 16$ or $\frac{4.5}{15} \times 9$ (or frequency density × width, e.g. $0 . 8 \times 10 . 5$).
> 
> **M1**: Their two partial amounts added to 4.
> 
> **A1**: A single whole number from 14 to 16 (15 using boundaries of 20 and 40), with no approximation sign.

parts.problem_md:

![Cumulative frequency graph with test score from 60 to 130 on the horizontal axis and cumulative frequency from 0 to 160 on the vertical axis. A smooth S-shaped curve starts at (65, 0), rises slowly to about (90, 30), steeply to about (105, 112), then levels off to (130, 160)](assets/004-cumulative-frequency-graph-with-test-score-from-.png)

Use the graph to estimate the number of employees whose score is within 5 of the median score.
parts.solution_md:
The median is read across from a cumulative frequency of 80

$\frac{160}{2} = 80$

![Cumulative frequency graph of test score from 60 to 130, the curve from (65, 0) to (130, 160). A dashed line runs across from a cumulative frequency of 80 to the curve and down to a score of 100. Dashed lines run up from scores of 95 and 105 to the curve and across to cumulative frequencies of 50 and 112](assets/005-cumulative-frequency-graph-of-test-score-from-60.png)

*Median = 100*

**[B1]**

Scores within 5 of the median lie between 95 and 105. Read up from these scores to the curve

*Cumulative frequency at 95 = 50*

*Cumulative frequency at 105 = 112*

**[M1]**

The number of employees between the two scores is the difference

$112 - 50$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **62 employees**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Median from 99.5 to 100.5, with the reading shown on the graph.
> 
> **M1**: Cumulative frequencies read at their median − 5 and their median + 5, shown on the graph.
> 
> **M1**: The difference between their two readings.
> 
> **A1**: A single whole number from 60 to 64 (62 for a correct reading of the graph).

Use the graph to estimate the lowest score of an employee who is offered the course.

**Final answer:** **Lowest score = 117**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: 144 seen, or implied by a reading from a cumulative frequency of 144 on the graph.
> 
> **A1**: Score from 116.5 to 117.5, with the reading shown on the graph. A correct value with no reading shown earns 1 mark only.

Use the graph to estimate the highest score of an employee who is offered extra support.
parts.solution_md:

![Cumulative frequency graph of test score from 60 to 130, the curve from (65, 0) to (130, 160). A dashed line runs across from a cumulative frequency of 8 to the curve and down to a score of 78](assets/007-cumulative-frequency-graph-of-test-score-from-60.png)

parts.problem_md:
The lengths of time, $t$ minutes, of Susie's calls with her customers are summarised in the table, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are unknown frequencies.

| Time ($t$ minutes) | $4 < t \leq 8$ | $8 < t \leq 12$ | $12 < t \leq 16$ | $16 < t \leq 20$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | 16 | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ |

The table was used to draw the cumulative frequency graph.

![Cumulative frequency graph with time in minutes from 0 to 20 on the horizontal axis and cumulative frequency from 0 to 160 on the vertical axis. A smooth curve starts at (4, 0), rises slowly to about (8, 16), steeply to about (16, 136), then levels off to (20, 160)](assets/008-cumulative-frequency-graph-with-time-in-minutes-.png)

Use the graph to find the values of $a$, $b$ and $c$.
parts.solution_md:
Read the cumulative frequencies at the class boundaries 12, 16 and 20

![Cumulative frequency graph of time from 0 to 20 minutes, the curve from (4, 0) to (20, 160). Dashed lines run up from 12, 16 and 20 to the curve and across to cumulative frequencies of 56, 136 and 160](assets/009-cumulative-frequency-graph-of-time-from-0-to-20-.png)

*Cumulative frequency at 12 = 56*

*Cumulative frequency at 16 = 136*

*Cumulative frequency at 20 = 160*

**[M1]**

Each frequency is the difference between consecutive cumulative frequencies

$a = 56 - 16$

**[M1]**

$a = 40$

$b = 136 - 56 = 80$

$c = 160 - 136 = 24$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Cumulative frequencies read at 12, 16 and 20 (at least two correct), shown on the graph.
> 
> **M1**: A frequency found as the difference of consecutive cumulative frequencies.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 40$, $b = 80$ and $c = 24$.

parts.problem_md: Use the graph to estimate the interquartile range of the times of Susie's calls.
parts.solution_md:
There are 160 calls in total, so the quartiles are read across from cumulative frequencies of 40 and 120

$\frac{160}{4} = 40$

$\frac{3\times160}{4} = 120$

**[M1]**

![Cumulative frequency graph of time from 0 to 20 minutes, the curve from (4, 0) to (20, 160). Dashed lines run across from cumulative frequencies of 40 and 120 to the curve and down to times of 10.8 and 15](assets/010-cumulative-frequency-graph-of-time-from-0-to-20-.png)

*Lower quartile = 10.8*

*Upper quartile = 15.0*

Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile

$15 . 0 - 10 . 8$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **Interquartile range = 4.2 minutes**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Readings taken at cumulative frequencies of 40 and 120, shown on the graph.
> 
> **M1**: Upper quartile minus lower quartile, with an upper quartile from 14.8 to 15.3 and a lower quartile from 10.5 to 10.9.
> 
> **A1**: Interquartile range from 4 to 4.8 minutes, from correct readings.

parts.problem_md: Use the graph to estimate the percentage of Susie's calls that lasted longer than 10 minutes.
parts.solution_md:
Read up from 10 minutes to the curve and across to the cumulative frequency axis

![Cumulative frequency graph of time from 0 to 20 minutes, the curve from (4, 0) to (20, 160). A dashed line runs up from 10 minutes to the curve and across to a cumulative frequency of 32](assets/011-cumulative-frequency-graph-of-time-from-0-to-20-.png)

*Cumulative frequency at 10 minutes = 32*

The calls longer than 10 minutes are the rest of the 160

$\frac{160-32}{160} \times 100$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **80%**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: 160 minus their reading at 10 minutes, as a percentage of 160, with the reading shown on the graph.
> 
> **A1**: A percentage from 78% to 81%.

parts.problem_md:
Crystal is given an incomplete box-and-whisker plot of the lengths of 99 unicorn horns. She also knows that

the median length is halfway between the minimum and maximum lengths

the range is 2.5 times the interquartile range.

Complete the diagrams below to show that there are two possible box-and-whisker plots that fit this information.

![Two identical incomplete box-and-whisker plots, labelled Diagram 1 and Diagram 2, on a scale of length from 30 to 90 cm. Each shows a box from 56 to 72 with a whisker from 72 to 81, with no median line and no lower whisker](assets/012-two-identical-incomplete-box-and-whisker-plots-l.png)
parts.solution_md:
The whisker on the right ends at the maximum, 81, and the right-hand end of the box, 72, is the upper quartile. The left-hand end of the box, 56, is either the lower quartile or the median

Diagram 1: the box runs from the lower quartile, 56, to the upper quartile, 72

$\text{Interquartile range} = 72 - 56 = 16$

$81 - \text{minimum} = 2 . 5 \times 16 = 40$

**[M1]**

*Minimum = 41*

$\text{Median} = \frac{41+81}{2} = 61$

**[A1]**

Diagram 2: 56 is the median, so it is halfway between the minimum and 81

$\frac{\text{minimum}+81}{2} = 56$

*Minimum = 31*

**[M1]**

The range is then 81 − 31 = 50, which is 2.5 times the interquartile range

$2 . 5 \times ( 72 - \text{lower quartile} ) = 50$

*Lower quartile = 52*

**[A1]**

![Two completed box-and-whisker plots on a scale of length from 30 to 90 cm. Diagram 1: whiskers 41 to 81, box 56 to 72, median 61. Diagram 2: whiskers 31 to 81, box 52 to 72, median 56](assets/013-two-completed-box-and-whisker-plots-on-a-scale-o.png)

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: With 56 and 72 as the quartiles, range = 2.5 × 16 used to find the minimum.
> 
> **A1**: Minimum 41 and median 61.
> 
> **M1**: With 56 as the median, the midpoint condition used to find the minimum.
> 
> **A1**: Minimum 31 and lower quartile 52.
> 
> **B1**: Both diagrams completed accurately.

parts.problem_md:
The box-and-whisker plot below shows the masses, in kg, of the 99 unicorn horns.

![Box-and-whisker plot on a scale of mass from 0 to 12 kg: whiskers from 2.8 to 11.2, box from 7.6 to 10.2 with the median line at 9.2](assets/014-box-and-whisker-plot-on-a-scale-of-mass-from-0-t.png)

Crystal discovers that two masses were recorded incorrectly: 11 kg should have been 8 kg, and 9 kg should have been 10 kg.

Explain why at most one of the five values on the box-and-whisker plot will need to be changed.
parts.solution_md:
With 99 masses in order, the quartiles and the median are single values

$\text{Lower quartile:} \frac{99+1}{4} = 25 \text{th value}$

$\text{Median:} \frac{99+1}{2} = 50 \text{th value}$

$\text{Upper quartile:} \frac{3(99+1)}{4} = 75 \text{th value}$

**[B1]**

Look at where each change moves a value

*11 kg (above the upper quartile) becomes 8 kg (between the lower quartile and the median)*

*9 kg (between the lower quartile and the median) becomes 10 kg (between the median and the upper quartile)*

**Final answer:** **The minimum (2.8 kg) and maximum (11.2 kg) are not changed, and the number of masses below the lower quartile and below the median stays the same, so the lower quartile and the median do not change**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **One mass moves from above the upper quartile to below it, so the upper quartile is the only value that could change**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The quartiles and median identified as the 25th, 50th and 75th values.
> 
> **B1**: A reason why the minimum, maximum, lower quartile and median are unchanged.
> 
> **B1**: The conclusion that only the upper quartile could change, because a value has moved from above it to below it.

parts.problem_md: Explain why it is possible that the box-and-whisker plot will not change when the masses are corrected.
parts.solution_md:
![Box-and-whisker plot on a scale of mass from 0 to 12 kg: whiskers from 2.8 to 11.2, box from 7.6 to 10.2 with the median line at 9.2](assets/015-box-and-whisker-plot-on-a-scale-of-mass-from-0-t.png)

After the correction there is one more mass below 10.2 kg, so the new 75th value is either the old 74th value or the corrected mass of 10 kg

**Final answer:** **If the old 74th value is also 10.2 kg, it becomes the new 75th value, so the upper quartile is still 10.2 kg and the plot does not change**

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The new upper quartile identified as the old 74th value (the corrected 10 kg being smaller than 10.2).
> 
> **B1**: The condition that the old 74th value is equal to 10.2 kg, so the plot is unchanged.

parts.problem_md:
The histogram shows the loudest sound level, in decibels (dB), reached by the bark of each of the 180 dogs at a rescue centre. No scale is shown on the frequency density axis.

![Histogram with sound level in dB from 88 to 112 on the horizontal axis and frequency density on the vertical axis, with tick marks but no numbers. Bars: 90 to 94, 94 to 98 (the tallest), 98 to 104, 104 to 106 (the shortest) and 106 to 110](assets/018-histogram-with-sound-level-in-db-from-88-to-112-.png)

Estimate the number of these dogs whose loudest bark was between 99 dB and 107 dB.
parts.solution_md:
The area of each bar is proportional to its frequency. Measure the areas in large grid squares (each 2 dB wide) using the heights of the bars

$90 \text{to} 94 \text{:} 2 \times 4 = 8$

$94 \text{to} 98 \text{:} 2 \times 7 = 14$

$98 \text{to} 104 \text{:} 3 \times 3 = 9$

$104 \text{to} 106 \text{:} 1 \times 1 = 1$

$106 \text{to} 110 \text{:} 2 \times 2 = 4$

**[M1]**

The total area, 36 large squares, represents all 180 dogs

$\frac{180}{36} = 5$

*1 large square represents 5 dogs*

**[A1]**

The frequency density scale follows from this (for example, the first bar has frequency 40 and width 4, so its height is 10)

![Histogram with sound level from 88 to 112 dB and frequency density from 0 to 20. Bars: 90 to 94 height 10, 94 to 98 height 17.5, 98 to 104 height 7.5, 104 to 106 height 2.5, 106 to 110 height 5. The region from 99 to 107 is shaded](assets/019-histogram-with-sound-level-from-88-to-112-db-and.png)

Find the area between 99 dB and 107 dB, assuming the dogs are spread evenly within each class

$98 \text{to} 104 \text{class, from 99 to 104:} 2 . 5 \times 3 = 7 . 5$

$104 \text{to} 106 \text{class:} 1$

$106 \text{to} 110 \text{class, from 106 to 107:} 0 . 5 \times 2 = 1$

**[M1]**

Add the areas and convert to a number of dogs

$( 7 . 5 + 1 + 1 ) \times 5 = 47 . 5$

**[M1]**

A number of dogs is a whole number

**Final answer:** **48 dogs**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Areas (or relative areas) of all five bars found, or equivalent use of the total area.
> 
> **A1**: Correct scale: 1 large square represents 5 dogs, or frequency densities 10, 17.5, 7.5, 2.5, 5, or frequencies 40, 70, 45, 5, 20.
> 
> **M1**: Correct proportion of at least one partial class, e.g. $\frac{5}{6} \times 45$ for 99 to 104, or $\frac{1}{4} \times 20$ for 106 to 107.
> 
> **M1**: Their three parts added: 37.5 + 5 + 5.
> 
> **A1**: 48 (accept 47 or 48; a single whole number, with no approximation sign).

parts.problem_md:
Kungawo measures the lengths, in millimetres, of 23 earthworms that he finds in his garden. His results are shown in the stem-and-leaf diagram.

![Stem-and-leaf diagram with stems 3 to 7. 3: 2 6. 4: 5 8 8 9. 5: 1 2 2 3 3 3 4 5 5 7 8 9. 6: 0 2 4. 7: 1 3. Key: 4 | 2 means 42 mm](assets/022-stem-and-leaf-diagram-with-stems-3-to-7-3-2-6-4-.png)

Find the median and the interquartile range of the lengths.
parts.solution_md:
The diagram is already in order. There are 23 lengths, so the median is the 12th length

$\frac{23+1}{2} = 12$

**Final answer:** **Median = 53 mm**

**[B1]**

The lower quartile is the middle of the 11 lengths below the median (the 6th length), and the upper quartile is the middle of the 11 lengths above it (the 18th length)

*Lower quartile = 49*

*Upper quartile = 59*

Subtract the lower quartile from the upper quartile

$59 - 49$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **Interquartile range = 10 mm**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Median of 53.
> 
> **M1**: Upper quartile minus lower quartile, with an upper quartile from 58.5 to 59 and a lower quartile from 49 to 50.
> 
> **A1**: Interquartile range of 10 (or 8.5 to 10 from quartiles in those ranges).

![Cumulative frequency graph with speed in km/h from 0 to 100 on the horizontal axis and cumulative frequency from 0 to 80 on the vertical axis. A smooth curve starts at (20, 0), rises gradually to about (60, 28), steeply to about (80, 68), then levels off to (100, 80)](assets/073-cumulative-frequency-graph-with-speed-in-km-h-fr.png)

parts.solution_md:
The median is the speed halfway through the 80 vehicles, so read across from a cumulative frequency of 40

$\frac{80}{2} = 40$

parts.problem_md:
The speed limit on this road is 80 km/h. The police stop every vehicle that is travelling at more than 10% above the speed limit.

Use the graph to estimate the percentage of these vehicles that the police stop.
parts.solution_md:
Find the speed that is 10% above the speed limit

$80 \times 1 . 1 = 88$

Read up from 88 km/h to the curve and across to the cumulative frequency axis

![Cumulative frequency graph of speed from 0 to 100 km/h, the curve from (20, 0) to (100, 80). A dashed line runs up from a speed of 88 to the curve and across to the cumulative frequency axis at 74](assets/075-cumulative-frequency-graph-of-speed-from-0-to-10.png)

*Cumulative frequency at 88 km/h = 74*

**[M1]**

The vehicles that are stopped are those faster than 88 km/h

$80 - 74 = 6$

**[M1]**

Write this as a percentage of the 80 vehicles

$\frac{6}{80} \times 100$

**Final answer:** **7.5%**

**[A1]**

> 
> **M1**: 80 minus the cumulative frequency read at 88.
